entries.body_de: The trees closed around me like cathedral walls. Sunlight broke through the canopy in golden rays, catching dust motes that danced in the still air. I walked because there was nothing else to do — no map, no destination, just forward. The forest breathed: moss thick as carpet, bark rough as old hands, the smell of earth and time. The path climbed upward. I was tired, but the tiredness was distant, like something happening to someone else.

entries.body_de: By midday, the forest thinned. I could see sky between the branches — pale blue, endless. The path narrowed, then split: one way led down toward a valley where smoke rose in thin threads, the other climbed higher toward bare rock and wind. I chose the valley. The trees gave way to bushes, then to cultivated earth. Someone had been here. Someone was still here. The wind caught my cloak and pulled it wide — for a moment I felt like I was flying.

entries.body_de: I collapsed onto a moss-covered stone at the village entrance. My legs trembled. I emptied the small stones from my boots — finally. Through the gate, I saw the village: wooden houses climbing the hillside, smoke rising from chimneys, a windmill turning slowly on the hill. Maron stood by a glowing bakery. He saw me. I saw the inn. He simply nodded. That night, I sat by the fire in the stone cabin, watching the flames. Outside, the windmill turned slow against a sky full of stars. I had arrived.

entries.body_de: I sat on a stone in the village square, looked up at the windmill, at the wooden houses, at Maron's bakery, and felt my heart swell. I had made it. Through the Lost Woods, over the mountain path, into this village. I raised my hands and made a heart shape — for no one, for myself, for the journey. I was here. I was alive. I was finally home.

entries.body_de: I woke to the smell of bread and the crackle of the fire. Morning light filtered through the small windows of The Sleeping Hyrule Inn. My legs felt better after rest. Maron was already in his bakery next door — I could hear the familiar rhythm of dough being kneaded. I want to help him today. I promised myself I would earn my stay.

entries.body_de: At noon, I finally gathered my courage and walked into Maron's bakery. The heat from the ovens wrapped around me like a blanket. He looked up from his dough, those kind blue eyes questioningly. I gestured — may I help? He studied me for a long moment, then nodded toward a sack of flour. Then the girl with red braids burst in, barefoot as always, demanding bread for her mother. Maron handed her a loaf without a word. That was when I knew: this was my village now.

entries.body_de: Late afternoon, the village square was empty. I stood at the well, leaning against the stone pillar, watching the light change on the mountains. The wooden bucket hung still on its rope. It was the first moment all day I had been still. The bakery's warmth still clung to my sleeves. Somewhere up the hill, the windmill turned. This was not just a stop on the road. This was somewhere I could stay.

entries.title_de: The Bakery and the Windmill Path
entries.title_en: The Bakery and the Windmill Path
entries.body_de: At noon, I was elbow-deep in dough in Maron's bakery, the heat from the ovens wrapping around me like a second skin. My arms ached in a good way. Then Lily burst in, barefoot as always, gap-toothed smile first. Maron sent me up the hill to the windmill with grain sacks. The path was steep but my legs knew it now. At the top, Creek Grandmother was waiting, hands flour-white, eyes sharp. She taught me to listen to the grain as it poured into the millstone. The stones remember, she said. So do I.

entries.body_de: I woke before the sun, to silence. Not empty silence — the forest was breathing. I lay still in the hay, listening. Somewhere beyond the village, beyond the windmill, the trees were whispering. Creek Grandmother's words from yesterday settled into my bones: the grain whispers, the stones remember. Today I would listen. After the morning bread, I walked to the creek to wash the linens. The water was cold, my hands red, the village reflected in the slow current. The forest was listening. So was I.

entries.body_de: I woke before the bread smell, before the rooster even. The hay was warm where I'd slept, and the windmill turned slow in the dark sky — I could hear it from here, a heartbeat in the village. Creek Grandmother's words came back: 'The forest listens to those who listen to it.' I rose, dressed, walked to the bakery. The ovens were already glowing. Maron handed me the first dough of the day without a word. I was part of the village now. Not a guest. Not a stranger. Family.

entries.body_de: The first thing I noticed when I got to the bakery this morning was the pile. Not of flour. Not of dough. Of linens — aprons, dishcloths, the long sleeves Maron wears when she's working the ovens. They'd been piling up in the back corner for three days. I gathered them into a basket and walked to the creek. The water was ice-cold. My hands went red within seconds. I scrubbed, rinsed, wrung, laid them out on the moss to dry. The village watched from above. By noon, the linens were clean. Maron said nothing. He never did. But he nodded.

entries.title_de: Sixth Morning — The Gift of Listening
entries.title_en: Sixth Morning — The Gift of Listening
entries.body_de: I woke in the hay to silence — but not empty silence. The forest was breathing, the windmill turning slow on the hill, Maron's ovens already warming. Creek Grandmother's lessons settled deep in my bones: the grain whispers, the stones remember. Today, for the first time, the silence didn't feel empty. It felt full. Full of everything I had learned in five days. Full of the bread I had baked, the water I had carried, the linens I had washed. I knelt at the wooden door of the cabin and looked out at the village. It looked back at me.

entries.body_de: I found it on the way up. Not lost, not hidden — just there, lying on the flat top of a stone that looked like it had been waiting. Dark wood, almost black, the grain running vertical like veins. An ocarina. Four finger holes, one thumb hole, the shape of it fitting my hand like it had always been mine. I sat on a mossy rock and held it. The mountains stretched out below me, mist curling through the valleys, the village a small cluster of stone and wood far below. I didn't play it. I just held it. Some things you receive. You don't need to do anything but hold them.

entries.body_de: Afternoon, in the foothills above the village, I gathered what Maron needed: rosemary, thyme, a fistful of mountain sage. The basket on my back grew heavy. The air smelled of pine resin and warm stone. Down below, the village was just visible between the trees — Maron's chimney smoking, Lily running barefoot across the square. I tightened the straps, bounced twice to settle the load, and turned back toward home. Not my old home. This one. Kakariko.

entries.body_de: I woke before dawn, the promise from yesterday still clear in my mind — teach Lily what Creek Grandmother taught me. The village was still sleeping as I slipped outside, but Maron's ovens already glowed. I found Lily near the well, barefoot as always. She was kicking stones into the water, not listening. I knelt beside her, took her hand, placed it on the stone. 'Close your eyes,' I whispered. 'What do you hear?' She was still for a long moment. Then her eyes went wide. 'The water!' she said. 'I can hear it through the stone!' I smiled. Creek Grandmother would be proud.
